title: The Treasure-House of Eloquence: Calagurris, the Roman Courts, and the Twelve Books
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Calagurris, born where the Cidacos meets the Ebro
stops.date_confidence: No ancient source gives a year. Jerome's Chronicon supplies only the ethnic, Quinctilianus ex Hispania Calaguritanus; modern estimates run from the mid-30s to about 40 CE, and c. 35 is convention rather than record. Scholarship has also asked whether the town marks his birth or only his family's origin. Month and day are unrecorded and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: A son is born to a Roman family at Calagurris Nassica, the municipium set where the Cidacos comes down into the Ebro, in Hispania Tarraconensis. They name him Marcus Fabius Quintilianus. The town strikes its own coin, keeps baths and a circus and an amphitheatre, and sends the sons of its notables to Rome; the Latin in its streets is provincial and correct. The day goes unrecorded, and so do the house, the mother and the year. Jerome, writing three centuries later, calls him Calaguritanus, of Calagurris.
suggested_refs: The Roman municipium of Calagurris Nassica Iulia, its coinage and amphitheatre, under modern Calahorra

stops.name: Calagurris, the boyhood with no witness
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No autobiographical statement about his own childhood survives. The father is inferred from a single citation of an example credited to pater meus at Institutio Oratoria 9.3.73; the town's character comes from municipal history, not from Quintilian. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: He grows up in the Ebro corridor, in a town the empire's ledgers have no reason to mention twice. His father is rhetorically trained, or practiced enough that his son will one day set down a turn of phrase in the Institutio and credit it to pater meus, my father, and say nothing further about the man. No brother is named, no schoolmaster, no property. Book One of the Institutio will explain at length how an infant should be taught to speak, which nurse to choose, when the letters may begin. Whether any of that describes the house he grew up in, the text never says.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 9.3.73, the single sentence in which Quintilian mentions his father

stops.name: Rome, brought up the road to the city
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. That he was in Rome as a young man is certain from his own recollections of hearing Domitius Afer, dead in 59. When he came, at whose expense, and with whom is nowhere stated. The year orders the segment only.
stops.campa: He comes to Rome young, by whose arrangement the record does not say, and he is there in time to stand in the courts under Nero and watch the advocates work. The city he enters is the capital of a language he already speaks better than most of the men born in it. Provincials out of Hispania are filling the schools, the Senate, and soon the throne; Seneca of Corduba is the emperor's tutor and the most imitated prose stylist alive. Quintilian will spend his working life arguing that this way of writing is a disease.
suggested_refs: The Roman Forum and its courts under Nero, the schoolroom of Quintilian's youth
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria (autobiographical remarks on Domitius Afer)

stops.name: Rome, the grammarian's bench
stops.date_confidence: Tradition. Later scholia name Quintus Remmius Palaemon as his teacher; the chronology permits it and Quintilian never confirms it. His criticism of the declamation schools comes from Book 2 of the Institutio, written forty years afterward, not from a statement about his own schooling. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He is put through the grammarian's course: the Greek and Latin poets construed line by line, scansion, correct speech, the first exercises toward declamation. A later scholiast names Quintus Remmius Palaemon, the most celebrated and most disreputable grammarian of the age, as his master. What Quintilian himself records, decades on, is what the schools of his youth were becoming, and he records it as a complaint: boys applauded for epigrams, drilled to dazzle a room before they could divide a case.
suggested_refs: The grammarian's curriculum of first-century Rome, described from the inside in Institutio Oratoria Book 1
sources: Later scholiastic tradition on Quintilian's teachers (via Wikipedia, 'Quintilian')

stops.name: Rome, the Forum, hearing Domitius Afer
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he heard and admired Afer, from his own autobiographical remarks in the Institutio; Afer died in 59, so the hearing falls before that. The specific year is a placement, not a record.
stops.campa: In the courts he finds his model: Gnaeus Domitius Afer, the sharpest forensic wit of the age and a man with an informer's record behind him. Quintilian listens, remembers, and will quote Afer's sayings and his handling of a case for the rest of his life. He watches him late as well, when the old orator keeps rising to speak past the point at which he should stop, and takes a lesson out of it that he sets down in the Institutio: an advocate has to know the hour to leave the Forum.
suggested_refs: Domitius Afer's sayings, preserved almost entirely because Quintilian wrote them down
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria (autobiographical remarks on Domitius Afer, including his late decline)

stops.name: Rome, Afer dies and the record loses him
stops.date_confidence: Afer's death in 59 is standard ancient chronology. Quintilian's own location that year is not stated anywhere; Rome is inferred from Afer's career base, not attested.
stops.campa: Domitius Afer dies, and with him goes Quintilian's last living link to the oratory of the generation before his own. Everything the young man has learned so far he has learned by standing in a courtroom and listening, which is exactly the education Book Ten will prescribe: hear the best men alive, then go home and write. After this the record loses him. He is not mentioned again for the better part of a decade, until the year the troops in Hispania hail Galba.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria Book 10, on hearing living orators as part of the training

segments.name: The Undocumented Decade and the Return with Galba

stops.name: Hispania, the years nobody wrote down
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the weakest stretch of the whole life. Tradition sends him back to Hispania to practice law between Afer's death and 68; no surviving contemporary source names his residence, a case, or an occupation. The pin is his birthplace because that is where the tradition puts him, and the tradition rests on Jerome's ethnic and nothing else.
stops.campa: For something close to nine years there is nothing. Tradition sends him home to Hispania to practice law in the provincial courts. No contemporary document places him anywhere, names a client, records a fee, or reports a word he said in any of it. He is somewhere between twenty-four and thirty-three, the years in which a Roman advocate is supposed to be building the reputation he will live on. This is the largest gap in the record of his life, and it sits directly in front of the decade that made him.
suggested_refs: The undocumented Hispanic decade, c. 59-68, of Quintilian's biography
sources: Jerome, Chronicon (the sole basis for the Hispanic connection)

stops.name: Tarraco, the governor who left for Rome
stops.date_confidence: Galba's governorship of Hispania Tarraconensis from 59 or 60, his acclamation by the troops at Carthago Nova in April 68, his receipt of the news of Nero's death at Clunia, and the Senate's proclamation at Rome on 8 June 68 are all attested. Quintilian's presence in his entourage is tradition only; Quintilian never states it. The April date follows the acclamation, not any record of Quintilian.
stops.campa: Servius Sulpicius Galba has governed Hispania Tarraconensis from its capital at Tarraco since 59 or 60, eight years of a province run at arm's length from Nero. In April his troops hail him; he refuses the imperial title and calls himself legate of the Senate and the Roman People. At Clunia the news of Nero's death reaches him. On the eighth of June the Senate proclaims him at Rome. Quintilian is said to have travelled in his train. Quintilian nowhere says so.
suggested_refs: Tarraco, capital of Hispania Tarraconensis, seat of Galba's eight-year governorship

stops.name: Rome, arrival in the year of the four emperors
stops.date_confidence: The 68 return to Rome is tradition, traced back through Jerome's identification of his Spanish origin; the month is a placement. The political chronology of 68-69 is standard and attested.
stops.campa: He arrives in a city where the throne is about to change hands four times in eighteen months. Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian: the succession has just been shown to the provinces as a thing armies decide, and the schools of rhetoric go on meeting through all of it, term after term. Whatever brought him back, patronage or the collapse of business at home, he is in Rome for the whole convulsion, past thirty, with no recorded achievement of any kind behind him.
suggested_refs: The Year of the Four Emperors, 68-69, the political weather of Quintilian's return

stops.name: Rome, Galba cut down in the Forum
stops.date_confidence: Galba's assassination in January 69 is attested standard chronology. Quintilian's connection to Galba is tradition, so the loss of a patron here is inference resting on inference; he appears in no account of the year's politics at all.
stops.campa: In January the Praetorians cut Galba down in the Forum and set Otho in his place; before the year is out Otho is dead too, and Vitellius, and Vespasian holds the city. If the tradition is right and Quintilian came to Rome in Galba's train, the protection lasted five months. He appears in no account of the year's politics, on any side, and afterwards names no patron for this period. The next thing the record states plainly about him is that he opens a school in the city.
suggested_refs: The murder of Galba in the Roman Forum, January 69

stops.name: Rome, the school opens
stops.date_confidence: The twenty years of teaching are Quintilian's own statement in the preface to Book 1. The start year is derived by counting back from a retirement placed at 88-89, not given directly by any source; the month is a placement. The school's location and fees are unrecorded.
stops.campa: He opens a public school of rhetoric in the city and begins the twenty years he will one day count off in a single sentence at the head of the Institutio. The work is daily and unglamorous: declamation themes set and corrected, boys of thirteen taught to divide a case, the same faults heard and named again every term. He is teaching the sons of the men who will govern the empire under the Flavians. Nothing in the surviving text says where the school stood or what he charged.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 1, the twenty years of teaching counted in one sentence
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 1

stops.name: Rome, the treasury begins to pay the rhetors
stops.date_confidence: The institution is attested at Suetonius, Vespasian 18, which gives 100,000 sesterces annually to Latin and Greek rhetors from the fiscus and gives NO year. The conventional 72 is a modern placement. Suetonius does not name Quintilian anywhere in the Life of Vespasian. Jerome's Chronicon separately makes Quintilian the first at Rome to hold a public school and salary, and Jerome's notice is placed by some reckonings as late as 88, in tension with the 72 convention used here. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: Vespasian, whose reign began as the last throw of a civil war, establishes an annual hundred thousand sesterces from the fiscus for the leading teachers of Latin and Greek rhetoric at Rome. It is the first public salary any teacher in the empire receives. Suetonius records the institution and names no holder of it. Three centuries later Jerome writes that Quintilian of Calagurris was the first at Rome to hold a public school and draw pay from the imperial purse. The two statements have been welded together ever since by everyone except the sources.
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Vespasian 18: Primus e fisco Latinis Graecisque rhetoribus annua centena constituit

stops.name: Rome, the Basilica Julia, pleading while teaching
stops.date_confidence: That he pleaded as an advocate alongside his teaching is attested by the first-person case references scattered through the Institutio. The Basilica Julia is an inference: the centumviral court most associated with advocates of his kind met there, but Quintilian never names the building. The year orders the segment.
stops.campa: He does not stop appearing in court. The Institutio is full of recollection from the advocate's side of the floor: judges who have to be handled, a rule of arrangement he learned by getting it wrong first. The centumviral court that hears the great inheritance disputes meets in the Basilica Julia along the south flank of the Forum, under the roof Augustus rebuilt, and that is the room an advocate of his standing works in through the seventies, with the school waiting for him afterwards. He never names the building.
suggested_refs: The Basilica Julia on the south side of the Forum, home of the centumviral court
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria (first-person case references throughout)

stops.name: Rome, the Palatine, pleading before Queen Berenice
stops.date_confidence: The case is confirmed verbatim at Institutio Oratoria 4.1.19, cited by Quintilian as an example of a judge with a personal stake. The year is NOT in the text; it is inferred from Berenice's residence at Rome under Titus. The Palatine setting is likewise inference from her imperial protection, not from the source, which gives no place. Charge, forum and outcome are unrecorded.
stops.campa: Berenice, great-granddaughter of Herod, sister of Agrippa II, and the woman Titus is said to have loved and put aside for the sake of Roman opinion, is living in Rome under imperial protection. Quintilian appears as her advocate in a case in which she herself sits as judge. He records it in Book Four in a single clause, and only as a technical instance of a judge with a stake in the outcome. The charge is not given, nor the forum, nor the verdict.
stops.quote: I myself, when I appeared on behalf of Queen Berenice, actually pleaded before her.
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 4.1.19, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 4.1.19, the only record that this case ever happened

stops.name: Rome, the benches of the school
stops.date_confidence: Pliny the Younger's association with Quintilian as pupil is widely accepted on ancient and later testimony, though the dossier does not name a single primary passage. Tacitus is often listed as a pupil and rests on nothing; he is named here only as an unsupported attribution. The year orders the segment.
stops.campa: The classroom fills with the sons of senatorial and equestrian houses headed for the courts and the magistracies. Pliny the Younger sits in it, and the association is carried by ancient and later testimony alike. Tacitus is often added to the roll and rests on nothing at all. To these boys Quintilian teaches that eloquence is not a trick of the tongue but a habit of the whole man, and that the habit is built out of reading, writing, and hearing the best living speakers, in that order and in no other.
suggested_refs: Pliny the Younger's letters, the principal witness to Quintilian's pupils
sources: Pliny the Younger, Letters (and later scholarly tradition)

stops.name: Rome, two books he never wrote
stops.date_confidence: The complaint is attested at Institutio Oratoria 1 pr. 7-8 and concerns two rhetorical handbooks taken down by pupils over a two-day lecture course. The lectures themselves are undated; the complaint is datable only to the moment of writing, c. 92-95. The year here orders the teaching segment.
stops.campa: Boys in his lecture room have been taking down what he says. Two books of it are now in the trade under his name, compiled out of a course that ran two days, sold as his work, revised by nobody. He opens the Institutio by disowning them, and the disowning is among his reasons for writing twelve books of his own: if the thing is going to circulate with Quintilianus on it, he would rather it were the version he wrote. The pupils who took the course down are not named. Neither of the two books survives.
stops.quote: two books on the art of rhetoric are at present circulating under my name, although never published by me or composed for such a purpose
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 1, preface 7, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The two lost pseudo-Quintilianic handbooks compiled by pupils from a two-day course

stops.name: Rome, Martial writes him a compliment on his way out the door
stops.date_confidence: Martial, Epigrams 2.90 is attested and addressed directly to Quintilian. Book 2 is conventionally dated to the mid-80s; the year here follows that convention rather than any statement in the poem. The English wording follows the Bohn's Classical Library translation of 1897.
stops.campa: Martial, who flatters nobody without a reason and few people without a barb, addresses him directly in the second book of the Epigrams. The poem is a refusal. Martial is declining Quintilian's advice to take up a proper career at the bar, and asking to be left to a small house, a full table, and an unhurried death. To make a refusal of that kind land, he first has to establish that the man advising him is the highest authority in Rome on what a young man should do with his life, which he does in the first line of the poem.
stops.quote: Quintilian, supreme ruler over our unsteady youth, Quintilian, glory of the Roman toga
stops.quote_source: Martial, Epigrams 2.90, trans. Bohn's Classical Library (1897), via tertullian.org
suggested_refs: Martial, Epigrams 2.90, the only contemporary poem addressed to Quintilian by name

stops.name: Rome, the rhetorician who owned estates
stops.date_confidence: The satire is attested (Juvenal, Satires 7.186-198) but was written a generation later, probably c. 110-120, and is not a contemporary witness. That Quintilian actually held vast estates is reconstruction: Juvenal's rhetorical purpose is to make him an exception, and no other source itemizes his property. The year places the wealth inside his own life rather than at the satire's date.
stops.campa: He is rich, and the wealth is conspicuous enough that a satirist can build a paradox on it: rhetoric is the trade that starves men, and here is a rhetorician with domains. Juvenal files him under rare good fortune, along with beauty, courage and noble birth, the things that happen to a man and cannot be taught. No source itemizes the property, and none accounts for it. Where does a schoolmaster get domains? The satirist raises the question and leaves it where it stands.
stops.quote: 'How then,' you ask, 'does Quintilian possess those vast domains?' Pass by cases of rare good fortune: the lucky man is both beautiful and brave, he is wise and noble and high-born
stops.quote_source: Juvenal, Satires 7, English translation via tertullian.org
suggested_refs: Juvenal, Satires 7.186-198, on the poverty of teachers and the exception of Quintilian

stops.name: Rome, twenty years done
stops.date_confidence: The twenty years of teaching are Quintilian's own statement in the preface to Book 1. The retirement year is not stated by him; 88-89 is the conventional placement, and Wikipedia gives 88. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He counts the teaching at twenty years and stops. The first preface of the Institutio says that friends had been pressing him for a book on the training of an orator, and that he had refused as long as he was in daily harness. He is somewhere past fifty. He has taught the governing class for a generation, pleaded before an emperor's mistress, drawn a salary from the treasury, and published nothing he meant to publish. Now he has otium, the leisure a Roman gentleman is supposed to earn, and no excuse left.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 1, the retirement into otium
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 1

stops.name: Rome, the Palatine, tutor to the heirs
stops.date_confidence: The commission is attested at Institutio Oratoria 4 pr. 2, which says only that Domitianus Augustus has entrusted him with the education of his sister's grandsons. Quintilian does not name the boys, does not mention the renaming, and does not name Clemens or Domitilla; the renaming to Vespasianus and Domitianus and the parentage come from Suetonius, Domitian 15. The Palatine setting is inference from the imperial household's seat; the text records the honour, not a place. c. 90 is conventional.
stops.campa: Domitian has no surviving son. He fixes the succession on the two young sons of his cousin Titus Flavius Clemens and of Flavia Domitilla, renames the boys Vespasianus and Domitianus after the founder of the dynasty and after himself, and hands their education to Quintilian. Quintilian records the commission at the head of Book Four, in the language of a man who understands precisely what has been set on him: Domitianus Augustus has entrusted me with the education of his sister's grandsons. He does not name the boys, here or anywhere else in the twelve books.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 4, the tutorial commission

stops.name: Rome, the consular ornaments
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The grant of ornamenta consularia through Flavius Clemens is recorded only by Ausonius, Gratiarum actio 7.31, three centuries later. No year is given anywhere; the date follows the tutorship. Wikipedia's statement that Vespasian made Quintilian a consul is a conflation of two different things and is contradicted here, not followed.
stops.campa: Through Flavius Clemens, the father of his two pupils, he receives the ornamenta consularia: the insignia, the precedence, the right to sit among men who have held the consulship, without ever having held it. Nothing of the kind had been given to a schoolmaster before. The grant is recorded by Ausonius, three centuries afterwards, in a speech of thanks for his own consulship, where Quintilian is the precedent he reaches for. Later writers turn the honour into an actual consulship and hand it to the wrong emperor.
suggested_refs: Ausonius, Gratiarum actio 7.31, the sole witness to the ornamenta consularia
sources: Wikipedia, 'Quintilian' (whose 'made a consul by Vespasian' is flagged as a conflation)

stops.name: Rome, the wife dead before nineteen
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6, which gives her age at death and nothing else. Her name, family, and the cause and exact date of death are unrecorded; the marriage date is inferred only from the book's place in the composition. The year here is a placement inside the probable 80s to early 90s range.
stops.campa: His wife dies before she has completed her nineteenth year. Her name is not recorded, nor her family, nor the cause. She had borne him two sons. In the preface to Book Six he writes about her at a length that a technical treatise on the training of orators has no occasion for whatever, and with a violence of grief that has embarrassed editors ever since: he calls his own survival unnatural, and says that going early spared her the thing that came next. He is writing after both of their children are dead.
stops.quote: Still her children survived her, and I, too, lived on by some unnatural ordinance of fate, which for all its perversity was what she herself desired; and thus by her swift departure from this life she escaped the worst of tortures.
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6, section 6, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6, the only record of this marriage
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6

stops.name: Rome, the younger boy, barely five
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Institutio Oratoria 6 pr. 6, which establishes the age and that he was the FIRST of the two sons to die. No interval between the mother's death and his is stated anywhere in the preface; claims that he died within months of her are not in the text. Name, cause and date are unrecorded; the year orders the segment.
stops.campa: The younger son dies first. He is barely five. His father sets down the age and the order and nothing else that would identify him: no name, no illness, no day. The preface to Book Six is the only document of this child's existence, and it exists because a man writing a technical manual on the training of orators broke off in the middle of it to say what had happened in his house. The book he is writing is a book about how to bring a boy up to speak.
stops.quote: My youngest boy was barely five, when he was the first to leave me, robbing me as it were of one of my two eyes.
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6, section 6, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6, the lament for the two sons
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6

stops.name: Rome, the elder boy at nine
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6: the elder son died at about nine, and the loss nearly halted composition. Name, cause and exact date are unrecorded. That the boy was one intended audience of the project, alongside the children of Marcellus Victorius, is drawn from the same preface and the dedication. The year orders the segment.
stops.campa: The elder son dies at about nine. Quintilian had meant the Institutio for him: twelve books as an inheritance, a father's whole course laid out for a boy already showing what he could do. He records the quickness, the voice, the seriousness beyond the years, the Greek pronunciation. He writes that he nearly stopped, that everything he had built the work on had gone, and that the friends who told him to go on were right. Then he goes on. Book Seven opens with the divisions of the issue.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6, and the dedication to Marcellus Victorius
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, preface to Book 6

stops.name: Rome, Book One, beginning at the cradle
stops.date_confidence: The content of Book 1 is attested in the text. The composition dates are not: the work is conventionally placed c. 92-95 on internal references to Domitian and the imperial heirs, and this year is a placement to order the segment. The argument against beating pupils is at Institutio Oratoria 1.3, standard content of the book but not itemized in the verified pool.
stops.campa: He begins the twelve books before the boy can talk. The nurse must speak correctly, because hers are the first sounds the child will copy; the tutor must be learned or say honestly that he is not; letters may be taught as play, with shapes cut in ivory; a class is better than a private tutor because a boy learns from other boys. He argues against beating students on the ground that a beaten child learns fear and learns nothing else. It is the earliest full Roman course of education from infancy that survives.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria Book 1, the earliest surviving full Roman curriculum from infancy

stops.name: Rome, Book Ten, the shelf gone through
stops.date_confidence: The Book 10 survey and its verdicts on Cicero and Seneca are attested in the text; the sentence that Cicero has become not the name of a man but of eloquence itself is at 10.1.112. That the Greek list opens with Homer and the Latin with Virgil is standard content of 10.1.46 and 10.1.85 but was not itemized in the verified pool and is carried here as reconstruction. The year is a placement.
stops.campa: In the tenth book he goes down the shelf and gives a verdict on everyone. Cicero, dead a hundred and thirty years, is set above them all: the student who has begun to take pleasure in Cicero has made real progress, because by now Cicero is not the name of a man but the name of eloquence. Seneca, dead thirty years and imitated by every young man in Rome, is handled with a care read ever since as a settling of accounts, ingenious and morally serious and ruinous to copy. Homer opens the Greek list, and Virgil the Latin.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 10.1, the comparative survey of Greek and Latin literature

stops.name: Rome, Book Ten, the hand before the voice
stops.date_confidence: The quoted sentence is verbatim from Butler's translation and stands at Institutio Oratoria 10.1.2, not at 10.3.2 as the research pool first had it; Butler's 10.3.2 reads differently. The composition date is a placement inside the conventional c. 92-95 window.
stops.campa: Reading, writing and speaking are one discipline in his account, and writing is the part that does the work. The pen builds what the tongue afterwards spends. Everything in the tenth book about what to read is subordinate to this: one reads in order to have something to write with. He is giving the advice in his fifties, having published nothing. He wants the student to write slowly and at length, to revise, to leave a draft alone and come back to it hostile, and only then to trust himself in front of a court.
stops.quote: eloquence will never attain to its full development or robust health, unless it acquires strength by frequent practice in writing
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 10.1.2, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 10.1.2 and 10.3, on writing as the foundation of eloquence

stops.name: Rome, Book Eleven, the treasure-house
stops.date_confidence: The phrase is verbatim from Institutio Oratoria 11.2.1. The composition date follows the conventional dating of the finished work to c. 95 on internal references to Domitian and the imperial heirs; no source dates the writing of an individual book.
stops.campa: The eleventh book comes to memory, the fourth of the five classical parts of rhetoric and the one that had never received a systematic Latin treatment outside the anonymous handbook addressed to Herennius. Quintilian opens with the phrase the schools already used, and then does what he does everywhere else: asks where it came from, who says so, and whether it actually works. What follows is one of the three surviving ancient accounts of trained memory, and it is the only one that argues with itself.
stops.quote: memory has been called the treasure-house of eloquence
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 11.2.1, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 11.2, the chapter on memory
sources: Rhetorica ad Herennium 3.16-24 (the anonymous parallel account)

stops.name: Rome, Book Eleven, the hall that came down at Crannon
stops.date_confidence: The narrative is attested at Institutio Oratoria 11.2.11-16, following Cicero, De Oratore 2.351-360. Quintilian's own scepticism about the two young men, on the ground that Simonides never mentions the episode, is in the same passage. The stop sits at Quintilian's Roman pin because the banquet at Crannon is Simonides's event and his place, not Quintilian's; nothing here stages Quintilian in Thessaly. The date is a placement.
stops.campa: He writes down the story that Cicero had written down before him, six hundred years after it is supposed to have happened, in a room in Rome. A poet named Simonides of Ceos sings at a banquet in Thessaly, is called outside by two young men who are not there when he reaches the door, and the roof comes down behind him on everybody else. He identifies the crushed bodies by remembering where each man had been sitting. Quintilian keeps the seating and doubts the young men: Simonides himself, he notes, never mentions any of it.
stops.quote: For he had scarcely crossed the threshold on his way out, when the banqueting hall fell in upon the heads of the guests and wrought such havoc among them that the relatives of the dead who came to seek the bodies for burial were unable to distinguish not merely the faces but even the limbs of the dead. Then it is said, Simonides, who remembered the order in which the guests had been sitting, succeeded in restoring to each man his own dead.
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 11.2.12-13, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 11.2.11-16, the fullest ancient telling of the Simonides legend

stops.name: Rome, Book Eleven, the authorities who disagree
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Institutio Oratoria 11.2.14-15, where Quintilian lists the disagreeing Hellenistic authorities by name and observes that Cicero's version had the wider circulation. The date is a placement inside the composition.
stops.campa: Having told the story he takes it apart. Was the banquet given for Glaucus of Carystus, for Leocrates, for Agatharcus, or for Scopas? Was the house at Pharsalus or at Crannon? Apollodorus, Eratosthenes, Euphorion and Eurypylus say one thing; Apollas, Callimachus and Cicero say another. He sets the names out in two columns, notes that Cicero's version gained the wider circulation, and declines to decide between them. The chapter never says which town he thought it was.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 11.2.14-15, the list of disagreeing Hellenistic authorities

stops.name: Rome, Book Eleven, places and images
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Institutio Oratoria 11.2.17-21. The quoted inference stands at 11.2.17, drawn from the Simonides narrative rather than contained inside it. The date is a placement inside the composition.
stops.campa: The method itself he sets out cleanly. Take a building you know, a large house with a forecourt and rooms and what stands in them; walk it until the order is fixed; convert each thing to be remembered into an image, and set the images along the walk, one to a place. Then walk it again while speaking, and each place gives back what was left there. The building can be used again indefinitely, because the images are wiped and the places are not. A public colonnade, a long journey or a painting will serve as well as a house.
stops.quote: it is an assistance to the memory if localities are sharply impressed upon the mind
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 11.2.17, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 11.2.17-21, the method of loci and imagines
sources: Frances A. Yates, The Art of Memory (1966), ch. 1-2

stops.name: Rome, Book Eleven, Metrodorus in the zodiac
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Institutio Oratoria 11.2.22, where Quintilian names Metrodorus of Scepsis and the three hundred and sixty loci in the twelve signs. Metrodorus's own career and reputation are known from other ancient testimony, not from Quintilian, who gives only the memory system. The date is a placement.
stops.campa: Metrodorus of Scepsis, ambassador, courtier of Mithridates, and by reputation the most formidable memory of the previous century, had built his system not in a house but in the sky: three hundred and sixty places distributed through the twelve signs, thirty to a sign, a memory palace with no walls and no floor. Quintilian records the figure and the method exactly, and records his own reaction to them as well. The verb he chooses is wonder, and he does not say that the wonder is admiration.
stops.quote: This makes me wonder all the more, how Metrodorus should have found three hundred and sixty different localities in the twelve signs of the Zodiac through which the sun passes.
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 11.2.22, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 11.2.22, the zodiacal memory system of Metrodorus of Scepsis

stops.name: Rome, Book Eleven, the reservation
stops.date_confidence: Attested in substance across Institutio Oratoria 11.2, where Quintilian's qualified critique of the loci method runs against the confident recommendation of the Rhetorica ad Herennium 3.16-24. The dossier summarizes the critique rather than quoting it; the wording here follows that summary, checked against the Loeb text of the chapter. The date is a placement.
stops.campa: He does not recommend it without reserve, and here he parts company with the handbook addressed to Herennius. An advocate in court has to improvise; a case turns on whatever the other side has just said; the images have to be invented beforehand and then held, which is a second memory to carry alongside the first. For long set speeches, he allows, the places may help. For pleading he trusts the division of the matter, rehearsal aloud, and the shape of what he wrote down.
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria 11.2, read against Rhetorica ad Herennium 3.16-24

stops.name: Rome, Book Twelve, a good man skilled in speaking
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Catonian formula opens Institutio Oratoria 12.1.1, and the verdict on the philosophers is at 12.1.18-19. That the perfect orator may never have existed is Quintilian's own concession in Book 12. The date is a placement inside the composition.
stops.campa: The last book turns from the technique to the man. He takes Cato's old formula, vir bonus dicendi peritus, and makes it the definition rather than the ornament: an orator who is not a good man is not an orator, because eloquence in bad hands is a public danger and because a liar cannot in the long run stay persuasive. Then he concedes that this person may never have existed. Of the philosophers he says they were great men who deserve veneration and who did not reach the highest perfection of human nature. The book is finished under Domitian.
stops.quote: The orator then, whom I am concerned to form, shall be the orator as defined by Marcus Cato, 'a good man, skilled in speaking.'
stops.quote_source: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 12.1.1, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb, 1920-22), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Institutio Oratoria Book 12, on the moral definition of the orator

stops.name: Rome, the Argiletum, Trypho takes the rolls
stops.date_confidence: The prefatory letter to the bookseller Trypho and the dedication to Marcellus Victorius are attested in the text; the finished work is conventionally dated c. 95 on internal references to Domitian and the imperial heirs. The Argiletum is inference: Quintilian names Trypho but no address, and the Argiletum is the known bookshop quarter of Flavian Rome. Month and day are placements.
stops.campa: The bookseller Trypho has been asking for the manuscript, and Quintilian has been putting him off. The prefatory letter that opens the finished work is the surrender: the books go over, with the remark that they will now have to take their chances in the world. Twelve rolls, addressed to his friend Marcellus Victorius and meant also for the education of Victorius's son Geta, go out from the shops between the Forum and the Subura, copied by hand, sold at whatever the trade will bear.
suggested_refs: The Argiletum bookshop quarter of Flavian Rome, between the Forum and the Subura
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, prefatory letter to Trypho and dedication to Marcellus Victorius

stops.name: Rome, Flavius Clemens executed
stops.date_confidence: The execution of Clemens and the exile of Flavia Domitilla in 95 are attested in the Suetonius and Cassius Dio tradition and are well established in standard reference works; the charge is described by ancient writers as atheism and adoption of Jewish practices. The fate of the two boys, and any consequence for Quintilian, is unrecorded. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Domitian has his cousin Flavius Clemens executed on a charge the ancient writers describe as atheism and a drift into Jewish practices, and exiles Clemens's wife Flavia Domitilla. Clemens is the father of Quintilian's two pupils, the designated heirs of the empire, and the man through whom Quintilian holds his consular ornaments. What happens to the boys is not recorded, and Quintilian's own text, which is all there is, says nothing about any of it. Whether anything at all happened to their tutor is not recorded either.
suggested_refs: The fall of the household of Titus Flavius Clemens, 95 CE
sources: Suetonius and Cassius Dio tradition on Clemens's execution

stops.name: Rome, Domitian killed in his bedroom
stops.date_confidence: The assassination on 18 September 96 and the subsequent condemnation of Domitian's memory are standard attested chronology. No ancient source states whether Quintilian was alive to see it; the Palatine pin follows the imperial residence, not any record of Quintilian's presence.
stops.campa: In September a conspiracy inside the household stabs Domitian in his own bedroom, the Senate votes his memory condemned, and Nerva takes the purple. The emperor who paid him, honoured him and gave him the heirs to teach is chiselled off the inscriptions of the city. No source says whether Quintilian was alive to watch it. He is not named in the accounts of the reign's end, nor in the accounts of what came after. The last securely dated fact of his life is a book published the year before.
suggested_refs: The assassination of Domitian, 18 September 96, and the damnatio memoriae that followed

stops.name: Rome, the record ends without a date
stops.date_confidence: There is no ancient death notice of any kind: no year, place, manner, will, tomb or epitaph. c. 95, c. 96, c. 100 and 'after 95' all appear in modern reference works and none is a record. Rome is assumed because his adult life was spent there, not because a source names it. The absence of any authenticated ancient likeness is a consistent negative across every source consulted.
stops.campa: There is no death notice. No ancient writer gives a year, a place, a manner, a will, a tomb or an epitaph. Modern reference works print c. 95, c. 96, c. 100 and after 95, and none of them is a record; they are estimates set in the typeface of dates. Rome is assumed because Rome is where the adult life was spent, not because a source says so. No authenticated portrait exists either. Every bust, engraving and statue labelled Quintilian was made by somebody who never saw him.
suggested_refs: The complete absence of an ancient death notice or tomb tradition for Quintilian

stops.name: Rome, the books that arrived under his name
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Spanish Wikipedia records two spurious collections attributed to him, 19 declamationes maiores and 145 minores. The figure of 388 for the original size of the Minor Declamations set is standard in the scholarship but could not be independently sourced in this pass and is carried hedged. The date is nominal, since the collections accrued over centuries and are not datable to a year.
stops.campa: Declamations begin circulating as his. Two collections survive: nineteen long ones known as the Major Declamations, and a hundred and forty-five of the Minor, out of an original set that scholarship puts near three hundred and eighty-eight. Both are judged spurious or composite by modern editors, and both kept his authority in working use for centuries in schools that had never laid eyes on the Institutio. The man who opened his own book by disowning two volumes taken down by pupils acquired, after death, several hundred more.
suggested_refs: The pseudo-Quintilianic Major and Minor Declamations
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 1 pr. 7-8 (his own complaint about spurious circulation)

stops.name: Rome, what became of the twelve books
stops.date_confidence: Later history of the object, placed at Quintilian's own pin and dated nominally to close the segment; the 1416 recovery was Poggio Bracciolini's journey to the abbey of Saint Gall and belongs to his own itinerary, not to Quintilian's, and is not staged as a scene here. Attested: mutilated copies circulated continuously in medieval France and Italy, chiefly as quotations inside other authors; Poggio found a complete text at Saint Gall in September 1416; Bruni's reply is quoted from Wikipedia's article on Quintilian. The editio princeps is ISTC iq00024000, Rome, Johannes Philippus de Lignamine, 3 August 1470, edited by Giovanni Antonio Campano; a second Rome edition by Sweynheym and Pannartz, edited by Bussi, followed within the month. The 'buried in rubbish and dust' phrase reaches us through secondary citation and is treated as tradition.
stops.campa: The Institutio does not vanish and it does not survive whole. Through the medieval centuries mutilated copies circulate in France and Italy, and scholars know most of the work as quotations lodged inside other men's books. In 1416, at a Benedictine abbey in the Alps, a complete text is found in a tower room, buried in rubbish and dust, and copied out. Leonardo Bruni writes to the man who found it that Quintilian has been delivered from a long imprisonment among barbarians. A printed edition follows at Rome in August 1470.
stops.quote: It will be your glory to restore to the present age, by your labour and diligence, the writings of excellent authors, which have hitherto escaped the researches of the learned... Oh! what a valuable acquisition!
stops.quote_source: Leonardo Bruni, letter to Poggio Bracciolini on the recovery of the Quintilian manuscript, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Quintilian'
suggested_refs: The complete Institutio Oratoria recovered at the abbey of Saint Gall in September 1416
The editio princeps: Rome, Johannes Philippus de Lignamine, 3 August 1470, ed. Giovanni Antonio Campano (ISTC iq00024000)
sources: CERL/ISTC incunabula catalogue, iq00024000 and iq00025000
Frances A. Yates, The Art of Memory (1966)

stops.name: Calahorra, the bronze in the birthplace
stops.date_confidence: The statue by Antonio Loperena Eseverri at Calahorra and the figure at Logroño in the Fuente de los Ilustres are both attested by Spanish Wikipedia, which gives no year for either. A date of 1970 appears in earlier research notes and is not confirmed by any source reached; the year here orders the segment and should not be quoted as a fact. No ancient likeness survives to compare either work against.
stops.campa: In the town at the confluence of the Cidacos and the Ebro, nineteen centuries after a boy was born there whose birth year nobody wrote down, a bronze figure of Quintiliano stands in the open street, the work of Antonio Loperena Eseverri. There is a second one at Logroño, among the sculpted worthies of the Fuente de los Ilustres. Neither resembles him, because nothing does. The town keeps the only thing that was ever securely his, which is the name of the place.
suggested_refs: The statue of Quintiliano at Calahorra by Antonio Loperena Eseverri
The Fuente de los Ilustres at Logrono
